newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore Jan exports weak on sluggish electronics.
newsitem.headline: Singapore Jan exports weak on sluggish electronics.

text.p: Singapore's non-oil domestic exports fell 3.1 percent in January year-on-year in nominal terms, reflecting a struggle to overcome sluggish demand for computer and electronic components, analysts said on Thursday.
The Trade and Development Board (TDB) said in a statement that January non-oil exports slipped again, following declines of 0.5 percent in December and 8.8 percent in November.
Non-oil exports totaled Singapore $7.36 billion (US$5.18 billion). In real terms, based on 1990 prices, non-oil exports rose 0.9 percent compared with December's rise of 4.6 percent.
A Reuter poll of 17 financial institutions on Wednesday had predicted a smaller year-on-year fall of 1.0 percent in the non-oil export data for January.
Analysts, however, said reaction to the figures on equities and foreign exchange markets was muted, with many expecting only a gradual pace of recovery in trade early in the year.
"The first quarter is going to be weak, with electronics being the biggest contributor as it comprises 67 percent of non-oil exports," Nomura's economist Maminder Singh said.
He said the data was "a bit negative", but no alarm bells were likely to sound as trade was seen to be recovering.
The Economic Development Board (EDB) said last month the electronics sector was expected to grow 10-15 percent this year after unusually slow single-digit growth in 1996.
As a result of the sluggish electronics sector, Singapore's economic growth slowed to 7.0 percent last year, from 8.8 percent the previous year.
But a brighter outlook is foreshadowed in higher U.S. orders for electronic parts and semiconductor equipment, likely to benefit Asian primary producers sometime around mid-year.
"If our trade figures don't show marked improvement by mid-year, that's when it won't be good for equities," said Fraser Securities research manager Violet Soh.
The TDB said total trade year-on-year in nominal terms was flat for January, against December's rise of 2.8 percent.
All major trade components, except oil exports, registered lower growth, with non-oil exports to the United States, Malaysia, Japan and Hong Kong remaining weak but improving to Europe.
Economists said the death of Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping was unlikely to affect Singapore's trade with China this year.
As in previous months, non-oil exports to China were strong at 54.1 percent and were expected to rise further this year.
"Exports to China have been improving because they've eased up on their credit policies and exports are expected to become stronger," Nomura's Singh said.
A silver lining was also noted in Singapore's import data, showing hints of an imminent economic recovery, analysts said.
"A recovery in the economy is usually preceded by import growth, given the nature of Singapore's economy," said Andy Tan, economist with MMS International of Standard & Poors.
He said the rise of 1.5 percent in imports to S$15.8 billion in January suggest exports would revive by the second quarter.
An economist with the National University of Singapore, Mukhul Asher, agreed. He said more imports in January were also being retained in the economy as re-exports had fallen.
"One encouraging sign is that retained imports have gone up," he said, adding that retained imports in a current month generally mean higher exports later.
